01.event: Rav Malkiyyu married a deaf-mute neighbor to a woman and had him write her a 400-dinar marriage contract from his property.
01.turn: Rava remarked on how wise Rav Malkiyyu was, giving his reasoning that a man would buy a maidservant for such a person, so a wife who is also a servant is all the better.
01.outcome: The contract stood and Rava endorsed the move.
01.summary: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu. Rav Malkiyyu married him to a woman and had him write her a marriage contract of 400 dinars from his own property. Rava praised him as a wise man, explaining that if the man would be given a maidservant to serve him, a wife who serves and is also a wife is a double benefit.

02.actor: A man who made an eiruv with onions, and Rabbi Meir
02.event: While Rabbi Meir spent Shabbat in Ardiska, a man told him he had made an eiruv with onions to walk to Tiv'in.
02.turn: Rabbi Meir did not accept the onion eiruv.
02.outcome: Rabbi Meir made him stay within his four cubits.
02.summary: Rabbi Meir once spent Shabbat in Ardiska. A man came to him and said he had set up an eiruv with onions so he could continue to Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir treated the eiruv as invalid and made the man remain within his four cubits.
02.missing: Why the eiruv fails is only inferred; the story is cited as a challenge to a legal ruling.

03.actor: Rabbi Zeira and then Rava, teaching in Mehoza
03.event: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd stoned him with etrogim.
03.turn: Rava taught first that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and was carried on silk, then taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret.
03.outcome: The people said he had forfeited his earlier honor, and Rava replied that he had done them good by widening their options.
03.summary: In Mehoza, Rabbi Zeira taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the converts present pelted him with etrogim. Rava taught the same town that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he then taught the mamzeret ruling too, they said he had lost the honor he had won; he answered that he had done them good, as converts could now marry from either group.

04.missing: Only a description of Rabbi Abbahu's habitual practice of carrying or not carrying a lamp depending on locale, followed by legal analysis of it; no single event.

05.actor: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, and his father-in-law Rabbi Yannai
05.event: Yehuda used to come home every Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire that Rabbi Yannai saw, but one day he stayed absorbed in study.
05.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, assumed Yehuda had died and had his bed overturned.
05.outcome: The remark came true like an error from a ruler, and Yehuda died.
05.summary: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, studied in the study hall and came home each Shabbat eve, with a pillar of fire going before him that Rabbi Yannai could see. One day he got caught up in study and did not come. Rabbi Yannai saw no sign and said to turn his bed over, since Yehuda would never have missed his time if alive. His words proved to be like an error from a ruler, and Yehuda died.

06.actor: A man selling glass beads and a woman
06.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it; she answered 'Give, give.'
06.turn: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' means nothing, since she was mocking him.
06.summary: A man was selling glass beads when a woman asked for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said only 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that such a phrase is nothing, as she was mocking him and did not agree, so there was no betrothal.

07.event: Rav Aha found his son Rav Ya'akov, whom he had sent to Abaye, was not sharp, and went to study himself, and Abaye arranged that he be forced to sleep in the haunted study hall.
07.turn: A seven-headed demon appeared to Rav Aha, and with each bow he made a head fell off.
07.outcome: The demon died and Rav Aha told the townspeople next morning that had a miracle not occurred, they would have endangered him.
07.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to study with Abaye, but found the son's learning dull, so he said he would go and study himself. Abaye, hearing he was coming, knew a demon haunted the study hall, and told the townspeople not to give Rav Aha lodging, hoping for a miracle. Rav Aha spent the night there, the demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off until it died. In the morning he told the townspeople they had put him in danger.

08.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah and asked how a wife is a man's helper.
08.turn: Elijah answered that she turns raw wheat and flax into bread and clothing.
08.outcome: The encounter ends with Elijah's answer.
08.summary: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked in what way a woman is a helper to a man. Elijah answered that a man brings wheat and flax, which he cannot eat or wear raw, and his wife prepares them, so she lights up his eyes and stands him on his feet.
08.missing: It is a brief encounter built around a question and answer, with no real turn or consequence.

09.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he replied that his daughter's sons are his sons.
09.turn: The Gemara explains he was only putting them off because he had become impotent from Rav Huna's discourses.
09.outcome: The reply is read as an evasion, not as a legal position.
09.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry a woman and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons count as his sons. The Gemara explains he was only brushing them off, as he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long discourses.
09.missing: Mostly a legal argument; the exchange is only a brief anecdote used as a proof.

10.event: Me'oret made her slave perform three of the dangerous acts and he died.
10.turn: This was raised as an objection to Abaye's ruling that out-of-order acts only weaken.
10.outcome: The Gemara explains that the slave was already weak.
10.summary: Me'oret once made her slave do three of the listed dangerous acts, and he died. This was raised as a challenge to Abaye, who said that doing them out of order only weakens a person. The answer was that the slave was weak to begin with.
10.missing: The incident is told in a single clause as a legal objection, with no detail of the event.

11.missing: Only rulings by Rav Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in reply to people being taunted as sons of Arameans; no event is told.

12.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, and Rav Ashi challenged him.
12.turn: Rav Ashi pointed out that several schools did not teach the lenient ruling.
12.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the challenge, as he relied on what he heard directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
12.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza. Rav Ashi asked what his basis was, noting that the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the lenient ruling. Ameimar still did not accept it from him, because he had heard it directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

13.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
13.event: In Rabbi's days the Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites into the congregation.
13.turn: Rabbi said that even if they permitted their own share, no one could permit the altar's share.
13.summary: In the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community. Rabbi answered that they could waive their own share, but nobody could waive the altar's share. The proposal did not go forward.
13.missing: The text implies but does not state that the proposal failed.

14.actor: A Roman man and a woman
14.event: A Roman asked a woman to marry him, she refused, and he ate pomegranates in front of her without giving her any.
14.turn: She swallowed her saliva and fell ill, and he then offered to cure her if she would marry him and she agreed.
14.outcome: He had her spit out her saliva while he ate, until something like a green leaf came out and she was cured.
14.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she said no. He peeled pomegranates and ate them in front of her, and her mouth watered so much that she swallowed it all and became ill. He then offered to cure her if she would marry him, she agreed, and he ate again while telling her to spit out her saliva. She did so until something like a green leaf came out and she was healed.

15.event: Ulla praised Rav Hamnuna as a great man, but wished Harpanya were not his city.
15.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed; Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and learned it was Pum Nahara.
15.outcome: Ulla concluded Rav Hamnuna was from Pum Nahara, not Harpanya, so his lineage was fine.
15.summary: Rav Hamnuna sat before Ulla studying, and Ulla exclaimed what a man he was, if only Harpanya were not his city. Rav Hamnuna was ashamed. Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and when he said Pum Nahara, Ulla said that makes him from Pum Nahara, so his lineage is unflawed.

16.actor: A man who deposited a goblet, and Rav Nahman
16.event: A man left a silver goblet in Hasa's house, and Hasa died without saying anything about it.
16.turn: The claimants came before Rav Nahman, who noted Hasa was not wealthy and the depositor gave a distinguishing mark.
16.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the depositor, with the caveat that it holds only if he does not regularly come and go there.
16.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet in the house of Hasa, who then died without leaving instructions. They came to Rav Nahman, who said he knew Hasa was not wealthy and that the depositor had given an identifying mark. He ruled for the depositor, adding that this holds only if the claimant is not someone who regularly came and went there.
16.missing: The ruling in favor of the depositor is implied rather than stated outright.

17.actor: A husband, his first wife, and Rava
17.event: A woman brought her husband two maidservants as dowry, he married a second wife and gave one maidservant to her.
17.turn: The first wife came before Rava and cried out.
17.outcome: Rava ignored her, since the house gained from the maidservant's work.
17.summary: A woman brought her husband two maidservants. He married another wife and gave one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came before Rava and cried out, but Rava paid no attention. Observers assumed he held that what the husband did was valid, but the real reason was that the household gained from it.

18.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he did so.
18.turn: Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna, Rav Ashi said that tradition says he did not rule, and Ravina answered that Rav Hamnuna ruled in the time of his colleague-teacher Rav Hisda.
18.outcome: Ravina argued that he too is Rav Ashi's disciple-colleague and so could rule.
18.summary: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he had done that. Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna, who ruled while Rav Hisda lived. Rav Ashi said the tradition is that he did not rule, and Ravina replied that both traditions are true, since Rav Hamnuna held back only during his main teacher's life, and he himself is a disciple-colleague of Rav Ashi.
18.missing: Rav Ashi's reaction to the final argument is not given.

19.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract, and Rava
19.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract on condition he would not reimburse if she objected.
19.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he came and objected himself.
19.outcome: Rava rejected the claim that he stands in his mother's place, since he had guaranteed against his own objections.
19.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract for a payment, and said he would not reimburse the buyer if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he came and contested the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he could stand in his mother's place, but Rava answered that though he had not guaranteed against her objection, he had guaranteed against his own.

20.event: Rabbi Zeira avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael.
20.turn: Rav Yehuda held that going up from Babylonia violates a positive commandment.
20.outcome: No outcome is given in the passage; the discussion moves to the verse debate.
20.summary: Rabbi Zeira wanted to go up to Eretz Yisrael, but his teacher Rav Yehuda held that doing so violated a positive commandment, so Rabbi Zeira kept out of his sight. The passage then turns to the scriptural debate between them.
20.missing: What happened to Rabbi Zeira, or whether he went, is not told; the passage cuts off into a verse citation.
